images.title: Two routes, same primes
images.purpose: Show that splitting 90 along two different routes ends with the same primes, only in a different order.
images.composition: Two small factor trees stand side by side, left and right of centre, with wide white space between them; two short caption lines sit centred under both.
exact_structure: Left tree (teal #0072B2 outlines): top circle 90; two branches down to 3 and 30; 30 branches down to 2 and 15; 15 branches down to 3 and 5.
Right tree (amber #E69F00 outlines): top circle 90; two branches down to 2 and 45; 45 branches down to 3 and 15; 15 branches down to 3 and 5.
In each tree the 4 end primes (left: 3, 2, 3, 5; right: 2, 3, 3, 5) are filled reddish purple #CC79A7 with white digits; composite circles (90, 30, 15, 45) are white with dark outlines.
Each tree has exactly 7 circles and 6 grey #6B7280 branch lines; the two trees together have exactly 14 circles.
Two caption lines centred under both trees: first Same primes, different order; below it 90 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5, with a small green #009E73 tick to its left.
rejection: either tree ends with primes other than one 2, two 3s and one 5
a tree with more or fewer than 7 circles
a composite number such as 15 or 45 coloured as a prime
images.takeaway: However you split a number, you always reach the same primes; only the order changes.
images.description: Two factor trees for 90, one starting 3 × 30 and one starting 2 × 45, both ending in the primes 2, 3, 3 and 5.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on writing a number as a product of primes.
images.teaching_notes: Compare the purple end circles of the two trees and count one 2, two 3s and one 5 in each.

image_decisions.why: Two trees side by side make the idea that every route ends in the same primes visible at once.
